deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 72 holds the end of a section of German prose notes on ancient (Sicilian/Greek) history. It continues the account of Agathocles of Syracuse begun on the previous page, where he is described as a potter's son who became general and, in 317 BC, king of Syracuse.

The text reads, roughly: 'In 311 he attacked the Carthaginians, who sent a large army under Hamilcar. He suffered a great defeat and had to flee into the city, where the Carthaginians besieged him. From this time on he became the worst tyrant, made repeated incursions into Lower (southern) Italy, but finally [died] in 289 by poison.'

The next page opens a new chapter, 'Dritter Zeitraum' (the Persian Wars to Alexander, 500–336). The bundle is therefore a set of history notes, apparently from a course or textbook in the style of Heeren's ancient history. The hand looks like a fair-copy or student hand rather than Gauss's characteristic script.

There are no derivations, computations or mathematical objects to reconstruct.
errors: The notes are historically compressed rather than wrong. They skip Agathocles' famous invasion of Africa (310–307 BC), which followed the defeat at the Himera/Ecnomus in 311 and the siege of Syracuse. Their phrasing could suggest he simply stayed besieged and then turned tyrant.
'Von dieser Zeit an wurde er der ärgste Tyrann' is an oversimplification. Agathocles' massacres of the oligarchs date from his seizure of power in 317/316, not only after 311.
Death in 289 BC by poison matches the tradition reported by Diodorus. Repeated campaigns in southern Italy (Bruttium, Croton) are also correct, so the notes contain no factual errors as such.

results.what: Historical narrative: Agathocles' war with Carthage (311 BC defeat by Hamilcar, siege of Syracuse), his campaigns in southern Italy, and his death by poison in 289 BC
results.modern_name: Standard ancient-history textbook material (Diodorus Siculus books 19–21 as transmitted through 18th/19th-century compendia)
results.usually_credited_to: Diodorus Siculus (ancient source); textbook presentation of the type found in A. H. L. Heeren and similar Göttingen historians

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical history notes, routine textbook content on Agathocles of Syracuse, and probably not even in Gauss's hand. It has no mathematical content of any kind.

checkable.asserts: Agathocles' kingship as dated in the notes (317 BC to death in 289 BC) spans 28 years, consistent with the traditional reign length.
22 years elapse between the 311 BC defeat by Hamilcar and Agathocles' death in 289 BC according to the notes' dates.
